results.title: With new website, Army wants to speed up testing timelines at select ranges for private sector
results.description: The Army announced a new initiative this morning intended to speed up the time it takes smaller defense contractors to test weapon systems by opening up four domestic U.S. military ranges and one abroad to industry for testing platforms such as drones, counter-drone systems, low-cost interceptors and long-range fires. Using a new website , companies can request a reservation at one of the ranges, which are: Dugway Proving Ground, UT West Cibola Range, AZ Camp Grayling, MI Camp Shelby, MS The initiative also includes a partnership between U.S. Africa Command and the Royal Moroccan Armed Forces for U.S. companies to use the Africa Multidomain Training and Experimentation Center (AMTEC) Multidomain Training Area in Morocco. The website will pair each company that requests a reservation with a “concierge,” or human to assist them with scheduling time. Companies will use their own internal dollars to conduct their own testing. Army Secretary Dan Driscoll, speaking to reporters remotely from Camp Grayling Friday, said service officials and companies that were conducting tests at White Sands Missile Range, NM, recently told him on average it takes 12 to 18 months to adequately test a weapon system. “That is not sufficient," Driscoll said. "And so, what the Army has spent the last eight weeks doing is partnering with our leadership to go look at what other assets do we have in addition to Camp Grayling.” The secretary said that he expects that a company will be able to get access to a test range within 30 days of requesting a reservation. Abby Denburg, an executive with the defense startup company Covenant Industries, said the company successfully tested its Anthem missile this week at the AMTEC, which is considered the “pathfinder” of the initiative. “Together, we demonstrated not only the purpose of the Anthem missile, but also a repeatable pathway now available to every company through testrange.army.mil,” she said. That test, in addition to one last month during the Army’s Project Convergence exercise in California, have validated the maturity of Anthem in representative environments, Denburg told reporters today. “Covenant is preparing to begin delivering production-ready assets to our manufacturing line at the beginning of 2027 and put Anthem into the hands of the operators that need it,” she said. The future of the defense industry, Denburg added, depends on these types of partnerships where “government creates opportunity for innovation, and in turn, industry delivers capability,” she said. “Covenant is honored to have been the first company to demonstrate this new pathway and looks forward to building on this momentum as Anthem moves from successful testing into production, fielding and operational capability,” she said. Driscoll emphasized that Covenant’s ability to go from showing up at the Morocco range and testing its product within 13 days is the type of test streamlining the U.S. is working on, in observing lessons from the war in Ukraine. “If you look at what Ukraine has done so incredibly well, it's this innovation through necessity, and it's innovation at the speed that is near or close to matching the commercial sector. And so, what we, the Army, are trying to do is break down every single barrier that we have put up over the last 20 or 30 years,” the secretary said.
